extraction.name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) dataset
extraction.description: This paper introduces Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) dataset, a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research. The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages. Additionally, we provide Language Models (LM) and baseline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models and for all the languages in our dataset. We believe such a large transcribed dataset will open new avenues in ASR and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research.
extraction.creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert
extraction.inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by (i) training acoustic models on in-house data, (ii) generating pseudo-labels with these models, and (iii) retrieving the original transcript by matching pseudo-labels to available book transcripts. This involved downloading audiobooks, segmenting audio, generating pseudo labels, downloading and normalizing text sources for audiobooks, and transcript retrieval.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The final training data is lower than the initial LibriVox data because: 1) text sources for some audiobooks may not have been downloaded, 2) candidate labels were filtered during the transcript retrieval stage, or 3) data was filtered while creating valid/test splits.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox, with most of the text data based on Project Gutenberg text data.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were segmented into 10-20 second segments using trained acoustic models. Text normalization involved NFKC normalization, removing unwanted characters (punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols), removing end-of-line hyphens, and filtering characters outside a language's valid unicode range. Post-processing for numbers involved aligning matched text from the book with pseudo labels and replacing numbers in the matched text with corresponding aligned words from the pseudo label. Heuristics were used to deal with hyphens and apostrophes in the text.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All audio data was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Books with corrupted metadata (missing title, speaker, or author info) were removed. Audios with multiple speakers were removed. Only the latest version of books sharing the same authors and title were kept. Candidate transcripts were filtered out if the Word Error Rate (WER) between the candidate transcript and pseudo label was greater than 40%. Language model training data was filtered to avoid overlap with development and test sets by removing books with similar titles (edit distance < 2) or more than one percent of 5-grams appearing in dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Pseudo labels for segmented audio samples were generated by performing beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model on acoustic models. True target labels were retrieved by splitting source text into overlapping documents, using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams to find best matching documents with pseudo labels, and then performing Smith-Waterman alignment to find the best matching sub-sequence of words. For high-quality development and test sets, human transcribers listened to audio files while looking at transcripts and corrected 'clear and obvious' errors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human transcribers were instructed to only correct 'clear and obvious' errors to avoid adding potential bias. Word Error Rate (WER) between generated transcripts and human rated transcripts was measured and reported.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Acoustic models (Time-Depth Separable Convolutions with Auto-Segmentation Criterion loss), 4-gram language models, wav2letter@anywhere framework (for streaming inference), pdftotext tool (for extracting text from PDFs/EPUBs), Smith-Waterman alignment algorithm, SVM with RBF kernel (gender classifier), KenLM toolkit (for training language models), wav2letter++ framework (for ASR baselines).
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender of speakers was labeled using a gender classifier and used for balancing development and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is expected to promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and in multilingual ASR. It can also be used for Text-to-Speech (TTS) research.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: For Polish, a high Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) rate (13%) negatively impacts Word Error Rate (WER) when performing Language Model (LM) decoding with a constrained lexicon. The final dataset size is smaller than the raw LibriVox data due to filtering steps (e.g., inability to download text sources, filtering candidate labels, filtering during train/dev/test splits).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is suitable for speech research, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research. It provides train, development, and test sets for model evaluation, and limited supervision datasets (10-hour, 1-hour, and 10-minute sets) for low-resource training benchmarks. It is also intended for measuring ASR system performance and for extending existing TTS datasets.
